Fix order of locale environment variable

During detection of the language to select translations the code is
[relying][1] on the same environment variables [libc][2]'s use, but
you are not considering them in the same order `glibc`
(and `gettext(3)`) do.

Specifically, you want to get the value of ``LC_MESSAGES`` locale
category (do not mistake here with the environemtn variable with the
same name).  To do that, the manuals says:

    If locale is an empty string, "", each part of the locale that
    should be modified is set according to the environment variables.
    The details are implementation-dependent.  For glibc, first
    (regardless of category), the environment variable LC_ALL is
    inspected, next the environment variable with the same name as the
    category (see the table above), and finally the environment
    variable LANG.  The first existing environment variable is used.

Furthermore, ``LANGUAGE`` is a GNU extension to be used as a fallback
for all those.

Following the above, this patch fix the proper order of environment
variable selection to consider `LC_MESSAGES` before `LANG`, and put
`LANGUAGE` as the last option.


 [1]: http://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/hardy/man3/setlocale.3posix.html
 [2]: https://github.com/bcoe/yargs/blob/master/lib/locale.js#L9

fix: restore parser state when a parse throws from .fail()

When a custom .fail() handler throws (or a command handler throws), the
synchronous path in parse() never reached kUnfreeze, so the frozen state
pushed for that parse was never popped. Separately, a command that fails
validation never pops itself off the command context.

The combined effect was that a reused yargs instance leaked the failed
command's positionals and context into subsequent parses: after a failed
'build' parse, an unknown command reported 'Missing required argument:
prompt' instead of 'Unknown commands: fly, away'.

Unfreeze on the throwing path, and truncate the command context back to
its depth at freeze time rather than assuming the pops were balanced.

fix: apply coerce on every parse of a reused instance

A yargs instance is documented as reusable across multiple parse() calls,
but the coerce (mutating) middleware set an applied flag that was never
reset, so coerce only ran on the first parse. The second and later parses
returned the raw, un-coerced value.

Reset the applied flag on mutating middleware at the start of a top-level
parse (commandIndex === 0) via a new GlobalMiddleware.resetApplied(). The
guard stays in place during a single parse, so the nested-command
double-coerce fix from #1966 is preserved.

Adds a regression test that parses one instance three times and asserts
coerce runs every time.

fix: route synchronous command handler errors through .fail()

A command handler that threw synchronously escaped Commander's error
handling entirely: unlike a handler that returns a rejected promise
(which is routed to .fail()), the synchronous throw propagated out of
maybeAsyncResult() uncaught, so .fail() was never invoked.

Wrap the handler invocation so a synchronous throw is routed through
usage.fail() exactly like the asynchronous rejection path, keeping the
existing behavior when a parse callback is registered.

The `check` validation test relied on the previous swallowing (its
guard handler threw but the error vanished); update it to assert that
the thrown check error reaches .fail(), consistent with the async path.

fix: resolve show-hidden key via camelCase when strip-dashed is enabled

When parserConfiguration({ 'strip-dashed': true }) is set, yargs-parser
strips dashed keys from the parsed argv and only keeps camelCase variants.
filterHiddenOptions was looking up the show-hidden option by its raw
(dashed) name, which is always undefined under strip-dashed, causing
--show-hidden to silently do nothing.

Fix: also check argv[shim.Parser.camelCase(showHiddenOpt)] as a fallback.
If the dashed key is present (normal mode) the first lookup hits; if only
the camelCase key is present (strip-dashed mode) the second lookup hits.

fix(choices): deduplicate when same value added multiple times

Multiple calls to `.choices(key, values)` with overlapping values
previously produced duplicate entries via a plain `.concat()`.

The docs say all enumerated values will be "merged together", which
implies a set union. This change wraps the concat result in `new Set`
before assigning so each choice value appears at most once.

Before:
  .choices('color', ['red', 'green', 'blue'])
  .choices('color', ['blue', 'rainbow'])
  // => ['red', 'green', 'blue', 'blue', 'rainbow']

After:
  .choices('color', ['red', 'green', 'blue'])
  .choices('color', ['blue', 'rainbow'])
  // => ['red', 'green', 'blue', 'rainbow']

fix (singletonify): parsed frozen to false (#1144)

singletonify() used to set Argv's properties to the singleton's
properties values _at the time of Argv's last call_.

So Argv's properties and the singleton's ones diverged
afterwards, such as parsed after a call to parse, still false
in Argv.parsed, not in singleton.parse.

singletonify() now adds setters to Argv instead, looking for the
value of the corresponding property in the singleton _at the time
the property is used_.

Make Dutch translation consistent, fix Dutch language errors, and make it real Dutch

- "Commands:" and "command" should be translated consistently (it was "Opdrachten:" and "commando"); "commando" is much more appropriate in this context than "opdracht"
- In Dutch, there is a difference between "nummer" and "getal". A "nummer" is used for the English "digit" ([0-9]). A "getal" is what is meant here (the type of all numbers)
- the translation of "boolean" is "booleaans"
- "string" was translated as "text". "text" is not a Dutch word. In Dutch, "text" becomes "tekst". But a string is not a text.
   https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/language/Search?&searchTerm=number&langID=Dutch&Source=true&productid=All%20Products translates "string" to "tekenreeks", but that is
   hypercorrect. Nobody uses that term. In Dutch, we just use the English term "string" colloquially.
- "Non-option argument" should be translated as "niet-optie-argument" ("niet" instead  of "non")
- The sentence aspect of "got %s, need at least %s" and "got %s, maximum of %s" was not translated sensibly
- "Missing argument value: %s" was not translated at all
- In the singular, there is no ending-'e' for an adjective if there is no article ("verplicht")
- The plural form "waarden" of "waarde" (value) seems more appropriate here than the alternative "waardes"
- The English word "check" can be used in Dutch to mean "validation", in the 1970's. In this century, we use "controle" colloquially. "Validatie", "verificatie", etc. are possible, but technical jargon
- "Implications failed:" is difficult to translate, because the English form is bad to start with. A literal translation is very awkward in Dutch. This string is used in the code as the
   prelude to a list of "implications" that have failed. A better English form would be "Failed implications:", and the new Dutch translation expresses that. Furthermore, the wordt "implications",
   in English, as well as in Dutch, is extremely confusing here. It is only people who know the Yargs API that understand that these are the dependencies created by the `implies()` method.
   Users of the CLI have no idea what we are talking about. Yet, until a better form is found in English, it is also kept in Dutch.
- In Dutch, we only know compound substantives, not concatenated substantives ("non-option argument" -> "niet-optie-argument", "Argument check" -> "Argumentcontrole", "JSON config file" -> "JSON-config-bestand", "version number" -> "versienummer")
- Since the orginal text talks about the "config file", referring to the name of the file (`config`), the translation should do so too. It was "configuratiebestand", which is Dutch for "configuration file".
- There is no direct translation in Dutch for the idiom "mutually exclusive". The unclear attempt at doing a direct translation was replaced by an idiom that is used in Dutch, that is more descriptive.

fix: $0 contains first arg on bundled electron app

Default behavior of yargs is to take the first two args of process.argv
to put into $0 as this is usually the program to execute a script
e.g. 'node app.js' but for bundled electron apps this results in $0
being populated with not only the executing program but also the first
parameter. This fix modifies the check for node/iojs (and adds electron)
so in case of those 3, the executing program is skipped in $0 as it was
before, but in case where a bundled app is executed, the first parameter
is skipped.

This is only a cosmetic change for proper help printouts which use $0
A manual yargs.parse(process.argv.slice(1)) is still necessary for
electron not to skip the first parameter, during parsing

Make Dutch translation consistent, fix Dutch language errors, and make it real Dutch

- "Commands:" and "command" should be translated consistently (it was "Opdrachten:" and "commando"); "commando" is much more appropriate in this context than "opdracht"
- In Dutch, there is a difference between "nummer" and "getal". A "nummer" is used for the English "digit" ([0-9]). A "getal" is what is meant here (the type of all numbers)
- the translation of "boolean" is "booleaans"
- "string" was translated as "text". "text" is not a Dutch word. In Dutch, "text" becomes "tekst". But a string is not a text.
   https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/language/Search?&searchTerm=number&langID=Dutch&Source=true&productid=All%20Products translates "string" to "tekenreeks", but that is
   hypercorrect. Nobody uses that term. In Dutch, we just use the English term "string" colloquially.
- "Non-option argument" should be translated as "niet-optie-argument" ("niet" instead  of "non")
- The sentence aspect of "got %s, need at least %s" and "got %s, maximum of %s" was not translated sensibly
- "Missing argument value: %s" was not translated at all
- In the singular, there is no ending-'e' for an adjective if there is no article ("verplicht")
- The plural form "waarden" of "waarde" (value) seems more appropriate here than the alternative "waardes"
- The English word "check" can be used in Dutch to mean "validation", in the 1970's. In this century, we use "controle" colloquially. "Validatie", "verificatie", etc. are possible, but technical jargon
- "Implications failed:" is difficult to translate, because the English form is bad to start with. A literal translation is very awkward in Dutch. This string is used in the code as the
   prelude to a list of "implications" that have failed. A better English form would be "Failed implications:", and the new Dutch translation expresses that. Furthermore, the wordt "implications",
   in English, as well as in Dutch, is extremely confusing here. It is only people who know the Yargs API that understand that these are the dependencies created by the `implies()` method.
   Users of the CLI have no idea what we are talking about. Yet, until a better form is found in English, it is also kept in Dutch.
- In Dutch, we only know compound substantives, not concatenated substantives ("non-option argument" -> "niet-optie-argument", "Argument check" -> "Argumentcontrole", "JSON config file" -> "JSON-config-bestand", "version number" -> "versienummer")
- Since the orginal text talks about the "config file", referring to the name of the file (`config`), the translation should do so too. It was "configuratiebestand", which is Dutch for "configuration file".
- There is no direct translation in Dutch for the idiom "mutually exclusive". The unclear attempt at doing a direct translation was replaced by an idiom that is used in Dutch, that is more descriptive.

fix: resolve show-hidden option lookup when strip-dashed is enabled

When parserConfiguration({ 'strip-dashed': true }) is set, yargs converts
dashed option names to camelCase in the parsed argv object. The
filterHiddenOptions function was looking up the showHiddenOpt key (e.g.
'show-hidden') directly in argv, but with strip-dashed enabled the key is
stored as 'showHidden' (camelCase), causing the lookup to always return
undefined and hidden options to never appear even when --show-hidden is passed.

The fix checks both the original key and its camelCase equivalent so that
show-hidden works correctly regardless of the strip-dashed parser setting.

fix: show-hidden displays hidden options when strip-dashed is enabled

When strip-dashed parser configuration is active, yargs-parser stores
parsed option values under camelCase keys (e.g. 'showHidden') instead of
the original kebab-case key ('show-hidden'). The filterHiddenOptions
function only checked argv[showHiddenOpt] using the original key, so
the lookup always returned undefined and hidden options were never shown.

The fix also checks the camelCase form of the showHiddenOpt key, which
is the key actually present in argv when strip-dashed is enabled.

fix: do not cap command help column at half wrap() width when no descriptions

The left column of a help table was always limited to half of `wrap()` so
that the right-hand description column would have room. For the Commands
table this cap was applied even when none of the commands had a
description, causing long command usage strings to wrap at half width
(and split onto a second line) despite plenty of horizontal space being
available.

`maxWidth()` now only applies the half-width cap when the table actually
has a right-hand (description) column with content. The dict form used by
the Options table is unchanged (it is always treated as having
descriptions), so option and example rendering is unaffected.

Some clarifying updates to de translation

Although I'm not a *native* German speaker (I *am* a native English
    speaker though), there were two specific
things that stood out in the translation as strange. (I will double
    check with native speakers if I have the chance -- and any native
    speakers, please share your thoughts.)

I did do some double and triple checking on word usage and other
translations, as well.

@maxrimue - I'm guessing that you're a native speaker of German, and you
contributed to the translation in the past - perhaps if you have a
minute you can review this?

* "count" - Based on the way that this would be used, I'm looking at it
as "a count of something" ... "a quantity of something" ... and for that
I think "Anzahl" would be a better choice. "Zähler" would be more of "a
counter" or "something that counts" (or even "someone who counts").

* "choices" - "Möglichkeiten" would more literally translate as
"possibilities" (to say "es ist möglich" is to say "it is
    possible/capable of happening/occurring"). But that's kinda what it
literally means - possibilities. "Auswahl" (and the verb auswählen - to
    choose, to select) would be a choice from a set of options. And
"optionen" would literally be the plural of "options"... I *suppose* one
could write "Auswahlmöglichkeiten" ... but to my ear and understanding,
      that would refer to the **availability** of **an opportunity to
      select something** not the **available selection options**
      themselves.
